title: Public Awareness, Trust, and Willingness to Engage with the Red Cross in Disaster Preparedness and Response: A Cross‐Sectional Study in Serbia
content: Humanitarian organizations depend on citizens who understand their roles, trust their actions, and are willing to participate in preparedness and response. This study examined public awareness, trust, perceived preparedness and effectiveness of the Red Cross of Serbia, expectations of humanitarian organizations, and willingness to engage in disaster-related activities. We analyzed a cross-sectional online survey of 155 adults in Serbia after item-level quality control. Composite scales showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.908-0.957). HC3-robust multiple regression indicated that awareness was the strongest independent correlate of trust (beta = 0.543, p < 0.001), perceived preparedness/efficiency (beta = 0.580, p < 0.001), and expected humanitarian role (beta = 0.545, p < 0.001). In the full engagement-readiness model, awareness (beta = 0.318, p < 0.001) and expected humanitarian role (beta = 0.346, p = 0.002) remained significant, explaining 45.9% of variance; trust was significant in the reduced model (beta = 0.253, p = 0.005) but not after expected role was added. Direct Red Cross contact was associated with higher awareness (Hedges g = 0.51) and readiness (g = 0.53), and nonparametric sensitivity analysis supported settlement differences in readiness. Pearson correlations showed strong overlap between trust and preparedness/efficiency (r = 0.884, p < 0.001), whereas readiness correlated moderately with interest in future participation (r = 0.478, p < 0.001). In ordinal logistic regression, a one-point increase in readiness was associated with 3.40 times higher odds of being in a higher future-interest category (95% CI [2.04, 5.65]). The findings indicate that actionable awareness, role clarity, and visible organizational value are central correlates of citizen engagement, while demographic differences are comparatively limited.
